raw.answer: A man convicted of a 1998 murder argued that a 2019 change to the statute of limitations, which removed the time limit for crimes causing death, could not be applied to his case. The Constitutional Court rejected this: it held the provision does not violate the ban on retroactive laws and does not breach the protection of legitimate reliance, and it dismissed his challenge to the court judgment and his request for interim relief.
raw.held: The provision (Article 8-2 of the Enforcement Act of the Criminal Code) is not a retroactive law and does not violate the principle of protecting legitimate reliance. The challenge to the judgment and the request for a temporary measure were both dismissed.

points.text: A new law is not truly retroactive if it applies to a situation that began under the old law and had not yet ended when the new law took effect.
Whether a limitation-period change is retroactive depends on whether the limitation period had already run out under the old law.

The provision applies only to crimes whose limitation period was still running, and does not revive crimes whose period had already run out. It merely extends the existing possibility of prosecution, so it is not retroactive.
The man's limitation period under the old law would only have run out on 17 July 2019, after the provision took effect on 31 May 2019, so applying it to him was not retroactive.

The legislature could choose, for important public interests, to remove the time limit for serious crimes causing death. Hoping the limitation period would soon run out is not a legitimate, protectable reliance.

Since the provision is not unconstitutional, the court's reading of it was not unconstitutional. His other complaints, about witness testimony and how the period is counted, were disputes over facts and law without a specific constitutional claim. The temporary measure was unnecessary because the case was decided.

who: People accused of serious crimes causing death whose limitation period had not yet run out
Prosecutors
Victims of serious crimes causing death
The man who filed the petition

raw.answer: Taiwan's juvenile case law says a court that receives a juvenile case by transfer may never transfer it again. A Hualien court asked whether this is constitutional, because the juveniles in its cases did not live in Hualien. The Constitutional Court held the ban unconstitutional where the receiving court is not actually the better place to protect the juvenile.
raw.held: The ban on re-transfer is invalid, from the date of the judgment, to the extent it applies where the receiving court cannot better protect the juvenile. The relevant authorities have 2 years to amend the law. Until then, the receiving court may re-transfer after investigating, and the juvenile or their representatives may appeal.

points.text: The juvenile law is the state's way of meeting its constitutional duty to protect juveniles' health and healthy growth, so it must serve the juvenile's best interests.
Transfers between juvenile courts must rest on real investigation showing the new court better protects the juvenile, and the juvenile must be able to state their views on where the case is heard.
The ban aims to stop courts passing cases back and forth and causing delay, so it is acceptable where the receiving court truly gives better protection.
Investigations can be incomplete or wrong, and a juvenile's living situation can change, so the receiving court may no longer be the best place to protect the juvenile.
A blanket ban leaves the court helpless in such cases, and the juvenile has no appeal or other remedy against the transfer order, which violates the constitutional duty of special protection.
In those cases the ban does not help its own purpose and is not an appropriate means, so it fails proportionality; the court also urged review of the lack of remedies against transfer orders.

who: Juveniles in protection cases
Juveniles' legal representatives and current guardians
Juvenile courts receiving transferred cases
Lawmakers and authorities who must amend the law

raw.answer: Several people said that as children or teenagers they were victims of sexual crimes, but prosecutors and courts refused to pursue their complaints because the time limit for prosecution had expired. Taiwan's Constitutional Court held that the old time-limit rule, applied to child and teen victims of these sex crimes, limits their right to seek prosecution too much, and it sent the cases back to the lower courts.
raw.held: The old Criminal Code Article 80 (before the 2005 amendment) is void from the date of the judgment, to the extent it counts time limits for child and teen victims of these sex crimes. The court quashed the applicants' final rulings and sent them back, rejected the other requests, and denied applicant 甲's request for a provisional order.

points.text: The right to sue in the Constitution includes the right of a crime victim to ask the state to investigate and prosecute. A time limit restricts that right, so it must meet the proportionality principle.
Sex crimes against children and teens harm important basic rights, and the state has a special duty to protect children's health and healthy development. Prosecution can also help victims recover.

Child and teen victims typically cannot report promptly because the crimes are hidden, they are immature, or family and authority figures pressure them. Delayed disclosure is a structural, normal pattern.
The old rule sets time limits by the maximum penalty and starts the clock at the crime. This ignores delayed disclosure, so much of the time runs out before victims can report.

The rule's purpose is legitimate, but it makes no adjustment for child victims, though alternatives existed such as starting the clock at adulthood or not counting time before a certain age. So the restriction is excessive and violates proportionality and the right to sue.

The decision is not retroactive for other pending cases whose time limit had already run under the old rule, to protect suspects' legal position. But in the applicants' own cases the lower courts must not count time before the victim turns 20, to give them effective relief.

who: Child and teen victims of sex crimes
The applicants whose cases were sent back
Suspects in sex-crime cases
Prosecutors and courts

raw.answer: Taiwan law required immigration-service companies to have their ads reviewed and approved by immigration groups designated by the National Immigration Agency before publishing, and imposed fines for skipping this. Two petitioners challenged the rules; one was a company fined NT$30,000 over Facebook posts. The Constitutional Court held the pre-approval system violates free speech and struck it down.
raw.held: The ad pre-review rule (Article 56(4)) and its fine provision (Article 79(1)(4)) are unconstitutional and lose effect on the day the judgment is announced. The Taipei High Administrative Court judgment against petitioner two is unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back to that court.

points.text: Truthful, non-misleading ads for lawful transactions are commercial speech protected by the Constitution's free speech guarantee.

Pre-review of speech content is a major intrusion on free speech, presumed unconstitutional in principle, and must meet strict review: a especially important public interest, a direct and absolutely necessary link, and prompt court remedies.
The rules are a real pre-review system. The designated immigration groups act with state authority, backed by fines and possible closure, so it is not mere industry self-regulation.

The purpose was to protect consumers from false immigration ads. This is a public interest but not an especially important one, because consumers can judge ads themselves and losses are usually financial.
The Interior Ministry's national-security claims (sham marriage, human trafficking) were not backed by any shown causal link between such ads and those harms.

Pre-review is not absolutely necessary: the Consumer Protection Act already makes businesses liable for ads, and other laws regulate false ads through after-the-fact penalties, which infringe less on speech.

The rules go beyond what is necessary and breach the proportionality principle, so they lose effect on announcement. The court did not examine whether immediate court remedies existed, and the final judgment was set aside as a consequence.

who: Immigration-service companies and their advertising
Consumers of immigration services
Immigration groups designated by the National Immigration Agency
Petitioner two (fined company) and its case

raw.answer: A company that paid large salaries to three people was supposed to withhold a supplementary health insurance premium and did not. It was fined three times the unpaid amount (NT$93,000) after it failed to pay by the deadline. Taiwan's Constitutional Court held that the fine rule can be unconstitutionally harsh in some cases because it uses the unwithheld amount as the only measure and applies a fixed multiple. The court gave the authorities two years to revise it.
raw.held: Article 85 of the National Health Insurance Act is unconstitutional to the extent that it measures the fine only by the amount that should have been withheld and sets a fixed multiple, which can be excessively harsh. The authorities must revise it within 2 years, and until then they and the courts may set a fitting fine in clearly excessive cases. The remaining parts of the petition were not accepted.

points.text: Fines limit property rights, so they must be proportionate and match the seriousness of the violation.
Past rulings say that when a law uses a single measure and a fixed multiple with no room for discretion, there must be a way to adjust and avoid excessive harshness in special cases.
The rule has a legitimate public purpose: saving health insurance resources, funding the system, and spreading premium burdens fairly.
The rule does take into account whether the amount was paid by the deadline and how large the amount was.

It ignores other factors such as how blameworthy the person was, how late payment was, and whether it was later corrected. A withholder who only assists in collecting premiums could be fined too harshly when the amount is large but the fault is slight.

Because the rule has no discretion, no reasonable cap, and no other adjusting mechanism, it violates proportionality and property protection to that extent. Until revised, the fixed 1x or 3x limit does not bind in clearly excessive cases.

who: Withholding obligors who fail to withhold supplementary premiums
The health insurance authority that imposes fines
Courts applying the fine rule
Insured people whose income is subject to the premium

raw.answer: A man was prosecuted for several related offences. Courts found him not guilty on some of them, and only the guilty findings (or other parts) were appealed. The higher court nonetheless sent the unappealed not-guilty parts back for retrial, and he was later convicted on one of them. The Constitutional Court ruled that the old appeal rule does not reach not-guilty parts nobody appealed, and that a 1940 precedent saying otherwise is unconstitutional.
raw.held: The pre-2021 Code of Criminal Procedure Article 348(2), which treats related parts of a judgment as also appealed, does not apply to parts where the original judgment found not guilty, and on that reading it is consistent with the Constitution. The part of Supreme Court precedent 29 Shang 3382 that treats unappealed not-guilty parts as appealed is unconstitutional, and the remaining requests were not accepted.

points.text: The principle that courts act only on charges and appeals brought before them protects defendants' right to a fair trial and to predict the scope of the case so they can defend themselves.
A prosecutor's view of how the charged facts should be classified does not bind the court. If the court finds some charges not guilty, there is no single-penalty rule linking them to the guilty ones.

The scope of an appeal is set by the parties and by the original judgment's reasoning, not worked out backwards from the appeal court's result. Unappealed not-guilty parts do not conflict legally with appealed parts.

Pulling unappealed not-guilty parts into the appeal would surprise the defendant, risk a second guilty verdict after a final acquittal, and let the prosecutor's charging decide the question instead of the court.

The precedent says unappealed not-guilty parts are treated as appealed, letting the appeal court go beyond what the parties asked. That violates the principle and the constitutional protections of personal liberty and the right to sue.

Requests about other rulings and precedents were not accepted because they were not applied in the case. Review of the court judgments themselves was barred because they were served before the Constitutional Court Procedure Act amendment took effect.

who: Criminal defendants acquitted on some charges
Prosecutors who appeal
Appeal courts
The applicant in this case

raw.answer: A defendant was detained by a trial judge, and the defense lawyer asked the court to cancel or change the detention on the defendant's behalf. The Pingtung court rejected this, saying only the detained person could do so. Taiwan's Constitutional Court ruled that this reading violates the Constitution, so a defense lawyer may make that request unless the defendant has clearly said otherwise.
raw.held: The rule on challenging detention orders (Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 416(1)(1)) is constitutional only if read to let a defense lawyer, unless the defendant has expressly objected, ask the court to cancel or change a detention order made for the defendant's benefit. The Pingtung court's ruling is unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back to that court for a new hearing.

points.text: Because three justices refused to take part in deliberation, the court deducted them from the total number of sitting justices, so it could still decide the case.
The application met the requirements for review, so the court accepted it.
Constitutional protections of personal liberty and the right to court access include the right of a defendant to timely and effective help from a defense lawyer.
Detention is the most serious intrusion on personal liberty, and a detained person is cut off from the outside and can hardly defend themselves, so depends on a lawyer.
A lawyer may already appeal a court's detention ruling for the defendant, and challenging a judge's detention order works in much the same way, so there is no reason to treat them differently.
The Pingtung court's ruling relied on a reading that conflicts with this, so it violated the Constitution and was set aside and sent back.

who: Detained criminal defendants
Defense lawyers
Trial judges and courts handling detention
The applicant in the Pingtung case
